overview.text: Apoptosis (uh-POP-toh-sis) is a regulated form of cell death—often called programmed cell death—that helps a multicellular organism remove unneeded, damaged, or abnormal cells. It is important in development and tissue maintenance: for example, it helps remove tissue between developing digits. Caspases, enzymes activated in a controlled chain reaction, carry out much of the cell’s dismantling. Signals can start the process through cell-surface receptors or from within the cell; one internal pathway involves mitochondria releasing cytochrome c. As apoptosis proceeds, the cell shrinks, its DNA and nucleus fragment, and its membrane forms blebs and sealed pieces called apoptotic bodies. Nearby cells or macrophages engulf these fragments. Unlike cells that swell and burst after acute injury, apoptotic cells are dismantled in an orderly way.

key_facts.text: Apoptosis helps balance cell production and removal, maintaining adult tissues.
Caspases activate one another in a cascade and cleave proteins involved in cell breakdown.
In one internal pathway, mitochondrial cytochrome c helps activate caspase-9 with Apaf-1.
In *C. elegans*, 131 of 1,090 somatic cells are eliminated through programmed cell death during development.
Apoptosis may be blocked in cancer cells, allowing abnormal cells to persist.
